claim: mESCs contain on average ~218,000 ± 24,000 CTCF protein molecules (mean ± std).
source: Quantification by 'in-gel' fluorescence revealed that, on average, mESCs contain ~218,000 ± 24,000 CTCF protein molecules (mean ± std)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 'in-gel' fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mESCs contain on average ~86,900 ± 35,600 Rad21 proteins and thus presumably cohesin complexes.
source: Quantification by 'in-gel' fluorescence revealed that, on average, mESCs contain ~218,000 ± 24,000 CTCF protein molecules (mean ± std) as well as ~86,900 ± 35,600 Rad21 proteins and thus presumably cohesin complexes (Figure 1B; Rad21 appears to be the least abundant cohesin subunit, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 'in-gel' fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: U2OS cells contain ~104,900 ± 14,600 Halo-CTCF proteins per cell.
source: Similarly, we determined the abundance of Halo-CTCF in U2OS cells (C32) to be ~104,900 ± 14,600 proteins per cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 'in-gel' fluorescence measurements.

claim: The CTCF abundance in human U2OS cells corresponds to about half the number of CTCF molecules determined for mESCs.
source: The CTCF abundance in human U2OS cells corresponds thus to about half the number of CTCF molecules determined for mESCs (~218,000 proteins/cell).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the measured CTCF abundances in U2OS cells (~104,900) and mESCs (~218,000).

claim: Independent FCS experiments in HeLa Kyoto CTCF-EGFP cells measured ~125,000 CTCF molecules per cell in G1-phase and ~181,000 in G2-phase.
source: Independent FCS experiments in HeLa Kyoto CTCF-EGFP cells measured ~125,000 CTCF molecules per cell in G1-phase and ~181,000 in G2-phase (Holzmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Holzmann et al., 2019).

claim: Cell-type-specific control of chromatin looping may be achieved in part by regulating CTCF abundance.
source: It is thus tempting to speculate that cell-type-specific control of chromatin looping may be achieved in part by regulating CTCF abundance.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed differences in CTCF abundance between cell types.

claim: FCS-calibrated imaging found a mean of 114,600 ± 10,200 CTCF proteins per U2OS interphase cell.
source: We found a mean of 114,600 ± 10,200 CTCF proteins per U2OS interphase cell, randomly sampling asynchronously cycling single cells (mean ± std of 4 replicates with number of cells n ≥ 21; 101 single cells in total; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FCS-calibrated imaging measurements shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Over 90% of cellular Halo-CTCF molecules localized to the interphase U2OS nucleus.
source: Over 90% of cellular Halo-CTCF molecules localized to the interphase U2OS nucleus (~106,000 nuclear Halo-CTCF molecules, which corresponds to a nuclear Halo-CTCF concentration of ~144.3 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,E)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FCS-calibrated imaging measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,E.

claim: The FCS-calibrated imaging result of ~114,600 ± 10,200 CTCF molecules per cell agrees within technical error with the 'in-gel' fluorescence estimate of ~104,900 ± 14,600 CTCF molecules per cell.
source: The result of our FCS-calibrated imaging method (~114,600 ± 10,200) agrees within technical error with our 'in-gel' fluorescence estimate of ~104,900 ± 14,600 CTCF molecules per cell, and thereby validates the latter approach for determining average cellular protein abundances.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from two different experimental methods.

claim: The best and final cross-validated estimate of CTCF abundance in U2OS cells is 109,800 CTCF proteins per cell.
source: We take the mean of the two methods, 109,800 CTCF proteins per cell in U2OS cells, as our best and final cross-validated estimate.
evidence: The claim is based on averaging data from two different experimental methods.

claim: The FCM estimate of mESC C45 Rad21-Halo is 131,800 ± 12,600 proteins/cell.
source: For mESC C45 Rad21-Halo, the FCM estimate of 131,800 ± 12,600 proteins/cell differed more from the 'in-gel' fluorescence estimate of 86,900 ± 35,600, but was still just within error.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FCM measurements.

claim: The best and final estimate of Rad21 abundance in mESCs is ~109,400 Rad21 proteins per cell.
source: We again take the mean of the two methods,~109,400 Rad21 proteins per cell, as our final, although less certain, estimate of Rad21 abundance in mESCs.
evidence: The claim is based on averaging data from two different experimental methods.

claim: The interphase cell cycle distribution of JM8.N4 mESCs is 10.2% in G1-phase, 73.9% in S-phase, and 15.9% in G2-phase.
source: First, we measured the interphase cell cycle distribution of JM8.N4 mESCs: 10.2% in G1-phase, 73.9% in S-phase, and 15.9% in G2-phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: The cell cycle distribution of JM8.N4 mESCs approximately agrees with other mESC estimates.
source: This approximately agrees with other mESC estimates (Hansen et al., 2018b; Sladitschek and Neveu, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to other studies (Hansen et al., 2018b; Sladitschek and Neveu, 2015).

claim: An 'average' mESC is approximately half-way through the cell cycle and thus contains ~3 genome copies.
source: This approximately agrees with other mESC estimates (Hansen et al., 2018b; Sladitschek and Neveu, 2015) and shows that an 'average' mESC is approximately half-way through the cell cycle and thus contains ~3 genome copies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured cell cycle distribution data.

claim: The fraction of CTCF molecules bound to specific DNA sites in mESCs is ~49%.
source: We have previously determined the fraction of CTCF molecules bound to specific DNA sites in mESCs by single-molecule imaging (~49%) and the total number of CTCF sites in the mESC genome by ChIP-seq (~71,000) (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: The total number of CTCF sites in the mESC genome is ~71,000.
source: We have previously determined the fraction of CTCF molecules bound to specific DNA sites in mESCs by single-molecule imaging (~49%) and the total number of CTCF sites in the mESC genome by ChIP-seq (~71,000) (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: An average CTCF-binding site is occupied ~50% of the time by a CTCF molecule.
source: Now we can use the information on the absolute abundance of CTCF proteins per mESC (217,200) to calculate that an average CTCF-binding site is occupied ~50% of the time by a CTCF molecule (always assuming three genome copies; full details in Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using measured CTCF abundance and previously determined binding site numbers.

claim: In the context of the loop extrusion model, the time-averaged occupancy of an average CTCF boundary site by CTCF is ~50%.
source: In the context of the loop extrusion model, this suggests that the time-averaged occupancy of an average CTCF boundary site by CTCF is ~50% (Figure 1G) – that is, an extruding cohesin will be blocked ~50% of the time at an average CTCF site in the simplest version of the loop extrusion model.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from calculated CTCF site occupancy in the context of the loop extrusion model.

claim: The fraction of cohesin complexes that are relatively stably associated with chromatin and thus presumably topologically engaged is ~40% in G1.
source: For cohesin, we previously estimated the fraction of cohesin complexes that are relatively stably associated with chromatin (~20–25 min residence time in mESC G1) and thus presumably topologically engaged to be ~40% in G1 (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: The upper limit on the density of extruding cohesin molecules is ~5.3 per Mb assuming cohesin exists as a monomeric ring or ~2.7 per Mb if cohesin forms dimers.
source: If we take this as the upper bound of putatively 'loop-extruding' cohesin complexes, we can similarly calculate the upper limit on the density of extruding cohesin molecules as ~5.3 per Mb assuming cohesin exists as a monomeric ring or ~2.7 per Mb if cohesin forms dimers (Figure 1G; full details on calculation in Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using measured cohesin abundance and previously determined chromatin-bound fraction.

claim: The calculated density of extruding cohesins corresponds to a genomic distance between extruding cohesins of ~186–372 kb in mESCs.
source: This corresponds to a genomic distance between extruding cohesins of ~186–372 kb in mESCs, which approximately matches computational estimates (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Gassler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from measured data and comparison with computational estimates from cited studies.

claim: A previous study used self co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP) of cohesin subunits to suggest a handcuff-shaped dimer model for cohesin.
source: Moreover, a previous study used self co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP) of cohesin subunits to suggest a handcuff-shaped dimer model for cohesin (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Zhang et al., 2008).

claim: Self-CoIP experiments of cohesin subunits in budding yeast and human HeLa cells could not detect cohesin dimers.
source: Still, this study has remained highly controversial (Nasmyth, 2011) and self-CoIP experiments of cohesin subunits in budding yeast (Haering et al., 2002) and human HeLa cells (Hauf et al., 2005) could not detect cohesin dimers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to other studies (Nasmyth, 2011; Haering et al., 2002; Hauf et al., 2005).

claim: Budding yeast condensin can extrude loops in vitro as a monomer.
source: Moreover, budding yeast condensin, an SMC complex related to cohesin, can extrude loops in vitro as a monomer (Ganji et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Ganji et al., 2018).

claim: Over-expression of the Rad21 subunit does not faithfully recapitulate the properties of endogenously tagged Rad21.
source: Since the mammalian study (Zhang et al., 2008) relied on over-expressed epitope-tagged cohesin subunits and given our recent observations that over-expression of the Rad21 subunit does not faithfully recapitulate the properties of endogenously tagged Rad21 (Hansen et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: In the C85 clonal line, the V5 CoIP clearly precipitated wild-type Rad21.
source: However, in the C85 clonal line, the V5 CoIP clearly precipitated wild-type Rad21 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The cohesin:cohesin interaction appears to be protein-mediated rather than dependent on DNA association.
source: This cohesin:cohesin interaction appears to be protein-mediated rather than dependent on DNA association since benzonase treatment, which leads to complete DNA degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), did not interfere with CoIP (Figure 2D; single-color blots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that benzonase treatment did not affect CoIP, as shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Rad21 either directly or indirectly self-associates in a protein-mediated and biochemically stable manner, consistent with cohesin forming dimers or higher order oligomers in vivo.
source: This demonstrates that Rad21 either directly or indirectly self-associates in a protein-mediated and biochemically stable manner, consistent with cohesin forming dimers or higher order oligomers in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CoIP experimental data.

claim: In the B4 clonal cell line, a V5-IP efficiently pulled down Rad21-SNAP-3xFLAG.
source: Again, a V5-IP efficiently pulled down Rad21-SNAP-3xFLAG (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In the B4 clonal cell line, a FLAG-IP pulled down Rad21-Halo-V5.
source: and, reciprocally, a FLAG-IP pulled down Rad21-Halo-V5 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Rad21 self-interaction was entirely benzonase-resistant and thus independent of nucleic acid binding.
source: As before, the Rad21 self-interaction was entirely benzonase-resistant and thus independent of nucleic acid binding as this enzyme degrades both DNA and RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing benzonase resistance, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At least ~8% of cohesin is in a dimeric state during the pull-down experiment.
source: Under the simplest assumption of cohesin forming dimers, we calculated that at least ~8% of cohesin is in a dimeric state during our pull-down experiment, based on our IP and CoIP efficiencies (full calculation details in Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from IP and CoIP efficiency data.

claim: The percentage of cohesin in dimeric state is likely an underestimate of the actual oligomeric vs monomeric ratio in live cells.
source: This percentage is likely an underestimate of the actual oligomeric vs monomeric ratio in live cells, since we expect a substantial proportion of the self-interactions not to survive cell lysis and the typically harsh IP procedures.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the effects of experimental procedures on protein interactions.

claim: A measureable population of mammalian cohesin may exist as dimers or oligomers.
source: Thus, while these results cannot exclude that some or even a majority of mammalian cohesin exists as a single-ring (Figure 2A), they do suggest that a measureable population may exist as dimers or oligomers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CoIP experimental data.

claim: The average protein copy number per cell is 460,517 ± 25,606 for Halo-Sox2.
source: To illustrate this, here we compared the background-subtracted TMR-fluorescence intensity of mESC lines carrying homozygously Halo-tagged Sox2 (Teves et al., 2016) and TBP (Teves et al., 2018) to our U2OS C32 Halo-CTCF cell line, and determined the average protein copy number per cell to be 460,517 ± 25,606 for Halo-Sox2
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FCM measurements using the U2OS C32 Halo-CTCF standard.

claim: The average protein copy number per cell is 99,111 ± 29,125 for Halo-TBP.
source: To illustrate this, here we compared the background-subtracted TMR-fluorescence intensity of mESC lines carrying homozygously Halo-tagged Sox2 (Teves et al., 2016) and TBP (Teves et al., 2018) to our U2OS C32 Halo-CTCF cell line, and determined the average protein copy number per cell to be 460,517 ± 25,606 for Halo-Sox2 and 99,111 ± 29,125 for Halo-TBP (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FCM measurements using the U2OS C32 Halo-CTCF standard.

claim: The FCM method may not be robust for very lowly expressed proteins (below ~10,000 proteins per cell).
source: Although this method should be generally applicable, we note that it may not be robust for very lowly expressed proteins (below ~10,000 proteins per cell; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and method limitations.

claim: The FCM method may not be appropriate for extremely highly expressed proteins (>10–20 million proteins per cell).
source: This will be instrument-specific, but we note that our method may not be appropriate for extremely highly expressed proteins (>10–20 million proteins per cell; calculated based on the LSR Fortessa instrument used in this study).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from instrument specifications and method limitations.

claim: Acute CTCF or cohesin depletion causes global loss of most TADs.
source: CTCF and cohesin have emerged as causal regulators of TAD formation and maintenance, since acute CTCF or cohesin depletion causes global loss of most TADs (Gassler et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Gassler et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).

claim: Knock-out of cohesin loading protein NIPBL affects TAD organization.
source: Concordantly, knock-out of cohesin loading proteins NIPBL (Schwarzer et al., 2017) and MAU2 (Haarhuis et al., 2017) also affect TAD organization, although to different extents.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Schwarzer et al., 2017).

claim: Knock-out of cohesin loading protein MAU2 affects TAD organization.
source: Concordantly, knock-out of cohesin loading proteins NIPBL (Schwarzer et al., 2017) and MAU2 (Haarhuis et al., 2017) also affect TAD organization, although to different extents.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Haarhuis et al., 2017).

claim: Loss of the cohesin unloader WAPL strengthens TADs.
source: Likewise, loss of the cohesin unloader WAPL strengthens TADs (Gassler et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Gassler et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).

claim: Models of genome folding through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is stopped by chromatin-bound CTCF, have been remarkably successful in reproducing the general features of genomic contact maps at the level of TADs.
source: Consistent with the key roles played by CTCF and cohesin, models of genome folding through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is stopped by chromatin-bound CTCF, have been remarkably successful in reproducing the general features of genomic contact maps at the level of TADs (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Fudenberg et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Fudenberg et al., 2017; Sanborn et al., 2015).

claim: Loop extrusion models have been limited by a dearth of quantitative biological data to constrain the modeling.
source: Nevertheless, these models have been limited by a dearth of quantitative biological data to constrain the modeling.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: The number of CTCF and cohesin molecules, the molecular mechanism of loop extrusion and the stoichiometry of cohesin during this process remain unknown.
source: Importantly, the number of CTCF and cohesin molecules, the molecular mechanism of loop extrusion and the stoichiometry of cohesin during this process remain unknown, further limiting our ability to test various models.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: JF646-labeling is near-quantitative in live cells.
source: We note that JF646-labeling is near-quantitative in live cells (Yoon et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Yoon et al., 2016).

claim: A titration experiment indicated ≥90% labeling efficiency for JF646.
source: moreover, a titration experiment indicated ≥90% labeling efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Rad21 appears to be the least abundant cohesin subunit.
source: Quantification by 'in-gel' fluorescence revealed that, on average, mESCs contain ~218,000 ± 24,000 CTCF protein molecules (mean ± std) as well as ~86,900 ± 35,600 Rad21 proteins and thus presumably cohesin complexes (Figure 1B; Rad21 appears to be the least abundant cohesin subunit, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured abundances of cohesin subunits.

claim: Essentially all endogenously tagged mRad21-Halo protein is incorporated into cohesin complexes.
source: Importantly, using single-molecule tracking we found that essentially all endogenously tagged mRad21-Halo protein is incorporated into cohesin complexes (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: The bacterial SMC complex, MukBEF, forms a dimer or 'dimers of dimers'.
source: Along these lines, the related bacterial SMC complex, MukBEF, also forms a dimer or and even 'dimers of dimers' (Arciszewska et al., 2019; Badrinarayanan et al., 2012; Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Matoba et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Arciszewska et al., 2019; Badrinarayanan et al., 2012; Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Matoba et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).

claim: The B. subtilis SMC condensin complex has been proposed to extrude DNA loops at a speed of ~50 kb/min as a dimeric handcuff complex.
source: Moreover, the B. subtilis SMC condensin complex has been proposed to extrude DNA loops at a speed of ~50 kb/min as a dimeric handcuff complex (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: In budding yeast, cohesin exhibits inter-allelic complementation consistent with a dimeric or higher order complex.
source: In budding yeast, cohesin exhibits inter-allelic complementation (Eng et al., 2015) consistent with a dimeric or higher order complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Eng et al., 2015).

claim: Previous self-CoIP experiments with differentially tagged budding yeast cohesin subunits failed to detect cohesin dimers or oligomers.
source: However, previous self-CoIP experiments with differentially tagged budding yeast cohesin subunits failed to detect cohesin dimers or oligomers (Haering et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Haering et al., 2002).

claim: Single-step photobleaching strongly indicates that budding yeast condensin can extrude loops as a single ring complex in a one-sided, asymmetric fashion in vitro.
source: Likewise, single-step photobleaching strongly indicates that budding yeast condensin can extrude loops as a single ring complex in a one-sided, asymmetric fashion in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Ganji et al., 2018).

claim: Budding yeast condensin can exist as both monomers, dimers, and oligomers.
source: Nevertheless, other studies have shown that budding yeast condensin can exist as both monomers, dimers, and oligomers and that multimeric budding yeast condensin is more active in a single-molecule magnetic tweezers-based DNA-compaction assay (Keenholtz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Keenholtz et al., 2017).

claim: Multimeric budding yeast condensin is more active in a single-molecule magnetic tweezers-based DNA-compaction assay.
source: Nevertheless, other studies have shown that budding yeast condensin can exist as both monomers, dimers, and oligomers and that multimeric budding yeast condensin is more active in a single-molecule magnetic tweezers-based DNA-compaction assay (Keenholtz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Keenholtz et al., 2017).

claim: Computer simulations suggest that only effectively two-sided extrusion can achieve the ~1000 fold condensin-mediated compaction observed for mammalian mitotic chromosomes.
source: Furthermore, recent computer simulations suggest that only effectively two-sided extrusion (either two-sided extrusion, or one-sided extrusion with directional switching) can achieve the ~1000 fold condensin-mediated compaction observed for mammalian mitotic chromosomes (Banigan and Mirny, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Banigan and Mirny, 2018).

claim: Mammalian cohesin contains either SA1 or SA2, but not both.
source: Since mammalian cohesin contains either SA1 or SA2, but not both (Sumara et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Sumara et al., 2000).

claim: SA1- and SA2-cohesin appear to mediate at least partially different functions.
source: and since SA1- and SA2-cohesin appear to mediate at least partially different functions (Kojic et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to another study (Kojic et al., 2018).

claim: Cohesin oligomers may be arising from cohesin clusters, which were previously observed with super-resolution microscopy.
source: These oligomers may also be arising from cohesin clusters, which we previously observed with super-resolution microscopy (Hansen et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to a previous study (Hansen et al., 2017).

claim: Folding of mammalian genomes into structures known as Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) is thought to help regulate gene expression.
source: Folding of mammalian genomes into structures known as Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) is thought to help regulate gene expression while aberrant misfolding has been associated with disease (Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Fudenberg and Pollard, 2019; Hansen et al., 2018a; Hnisz et al., 2017; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Symmons et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Fudenberg and Pollard, 2019; Hansen et al., 2018a; Hnisz et al., 2017; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Symmons et al., 2014).

claim: Aberrant misfolding of TADs has been associated with disease.
source: Folding of mammalian genomes into structures known as Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) is thought to help regulate gene expression while aberrant misfolding has been associated with disease (Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Fudenberg and Pollard, 2019; Hansen et al., 2018a; Hnisz et al., 2017; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Symmons et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Fudenberg and Pollard, 2019; Hansen et al., 2018a; Hnisz et al., 2017; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Symmons et al., 2014).

claim: The HaloTag is a popular and versatile protein-fusion platform that has found applications in a broad range of experimental systems.
source: The HaloTag (Los et al., 2008) is a popular and versatile protein-fusion platform that has found applications in a broad range of experimental systems (England et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Los et al., 2008; England et al., 2015).

claim: Endogenous Halo-tagging of proteins has become the gold standard.
source: Combined with the development of Cas9-mediated genome-editing (Ran et al., 2013), endogenous Halo-tagging of proteins has thus become the gold standard (Chong et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2017; Komatsubara et al., 2019; Rhodes et al., 2017a; Rhodes et al., 2017b; Stevens et al., 2017; Teves et al., 2016; Teves et al., 2018; Youmans et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Ran et al., 2013; Chong et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2017; Komatsubara et al., 2019; Rhodes et al., 2017a; Rhodes et al., 2017b; Stevens et al., 2017; Teves et al., 2016; Teves et al., 2018; Youmans et al., 2018).

claim: Endogenous tagging avoids the limitations and potential artifacts associated with protein overexpression.
source: because it avoids the now well-established limitations and potential artifacts associated with protein overexpression (Hansen et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2018; Teves et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Hansen et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2018; Teves et al., 2016).
